name: Hana Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana Ito, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines for years after a vocational certificate and apprenticeship. I'm experienced enough to know the North Lane circuit, but the pay is low for the trade; I like returning power to a whole street, and I worry when a callout disappears from the rota.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our gutter repair swallowed almost all our savings, and a utility bill is behind. My partner Kofi works care shifts that change each fortnight; our grown children have their own homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quicker report is welcome after a long repair, but the line still needs hands and a voltage test. That part is familiar ground for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried already, even if AI changes little. Our gutter repair used the savings, my pay is at the low end for this trade, and Kofi's care shifts change each fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the scheduled line repairs and ask payroll which callouts are available next month. In the first year Kofi and I would stop the weekly takeaway until the utility bill is caught up; I'd keep using the approved AI note helper only occasionally, after a job is done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady on a pole and tight in the stomach at the kitchen table. Less than a month's expenses in the account doesn't let me shrug off an ordinary bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was the last bill that surprised you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gutter repair exposed rotten timber underneath, and the invoice grew by two hundred. Our grown children helped carry the ladder, but they have their own rent and couldn't pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the note helper do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It turns my rough sentences into a tidy work record. I still compare the circuit number with the signed sheet before submitting anything.

say: I'd welcome **quicker reports** after long repair calls.
I'd say **hands and voltage tests** still decide whether a line is safe.
think: Our **gutter repair** erased the little savings we had.
My **low pay** and Kofi's changing care shifts keep ordinary bills stressful.
do: Take **scheduled repairs** and ask payroll about next month's callouts.
Stop the **weekly takeaway** until utilities are current; use the approved note helper only after completed jobs.
feel: **Steady** at work, tense over household money.
S0.quote: Less than a month's expenses in the account doesn't let me shrug off an ordinary bill.
fieldNote: Hana's **baseline money pressure** comes from a gutter repair, low pay and Kofi's variable shifts, not from AI.
Her **occasional note helper** follows the job and does not replace the signed circuit sheet or physical checks.

steps.text: Take scheduled line repairs and ask payroll about available callouts
Stop weekly takeaways until the utility bill is current

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company to let dispatchers test the new planning software before any roster is cut. Crews need the person who knows the locked gate as much as the person who writes a fast route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My field repairs will probably carry on, but the dispatch changes could cut the callouts we use to cover gaps in Kofi's care pay. With less than a month saved and only one other line depot nearby, that would hit quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the next union meeting I'll ask for a joint dispatch-and-crew trial and a written callout sharing rule. In the first year I'd try the approved fault map after dispatch has tested it, then keep the old feeder sheet beside it; we'd delay replacing our refrigerator unless it actually fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the hours but willing to test a tool that has passed real calls. The office staff shouldn't lose their voice because a screen looks tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which gate would you use in a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clinic lane has a chain after dark, and the dispatcher knows the caretaker's number. A route tool could save minutes or send us to the wrong side of the fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the refrigerator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The seal is worn, but it still keeps food cold. A new one would take the last bit of our account, so we can clean the seal and wait.

say: I'd seek a **joint dispatch trial** before roster cuts.
I'd defend **local gate knowledge** when routes are automated.
think: My **callout pay** could fall as dispatch work changes.
Our **thin savings** and few nearby depots leave little margin for lost hours.
do: Ask the **union** for a crew-dispatch trial and fair callout rule.
Try the **approved fault map** after dispatch testing; delay the refrigerator while it still works.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, willing to use a proven tool.
S1.quote: The office staff shouldn't lose their voice because a screen looks tidy.
fieldNote: Hana's **callout dependence** connects dispatch changes to household income and Kofi's variable care shifts.
She will **test the fault map** after experienced dispatchers, while retaining the feeder sheet and deferring a specific purchase.

steps.text: Ask the union for a joint dispatch trial and fair callout rule
Use the approved fault map after dispatch trials with the feeder sheet beside it
Delay replacing the refrigerator while the old one still cools food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union branch the thinking system in 2028 could rewrite dispatch and permits, but field robots around 2031 could take line repairs. We need paid placements before anyone cuts the people who know the circuits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when robots arrive, and I expect the company might drop a large part of my field hours. Kofi's hands-on care work could change too, while we have under a month saved and almost nowhere nearby to apply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union to bargain for paid safety-inspection placements and request my pension record, because I don't know what I could retire on. In 2029 I'd enroll in inspection training if the placement pays my wage; in the first robot year I'd apply for any posted inspection role here and ask the employment office about travel help for a distant vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lie awake trying to fit two lost pay packets against the rent. I can join the bargaining and apply, but I can't promise the company will offer a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kofi at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Kofi we should list the rent, medicines and travel before choosing any course. Our grown children can help us read a vacancy notice, but their wages belong to their own homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the placement teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want measured-voltage checks and what to do when a robot stops halfway through a repair. A certificate with only screen lessons wouldn't put me back into paid work.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 dispatch AI** from 2031 field robots.
I'd demand **paid inspection placements** before experienced crews lose hours.
think: At **63**, I expect a large cut in field hours.
Kofi's **care wages** may also change while our savings cover less than a month.
do: Ask the **union** for paid placements and request the pension record now.
Enroll in **paid inspection training** if offered in 2029, then apply for posted roles and travel help in 2031.
feel: **Sleepless** over likely lost wages and rent, despite a plan.
S2.quote: A certificate with only screen lessons wouldn't put me back into paid work.
fieldNote: Hana expects **major income loss** at the 2031 robot date and describes ongoing sleeplessness over rent.
Her **training condition** requires paid placement and physical safety content; scarce nearby vacancies may make travel support necessary.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate paid safety-inspection placements
Enroll in inspection training in 2029 if the placement pays wages
Apply for posted inspection roles when field robots arrive
Ask the employment office for travel help with distant interviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell management five years is enough to test robots with crews and negotiate what happens to the people doing repairs. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to stop climbing at 66, but I won't say so until I see the pension record. Our wages are modest, savings are nearly gone, and Kofi could still need the care job if robots reach that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd get my pension statement and ask the union to negotiate a paid trial role for experienced lineworkers. In 2032 I'd take that trial role if it pays at least my current wage; in 2034 I'd keep paid line work if available and apply for inspection shifts if retirement income falls short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried, but the years give us time to make a real budget. I don't feel safe enough to resign on a hopeful pension guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the budget include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, Kofi's medicines and travel to see our grown children. I would use a low estimate for his care shifts, not the best fortnight we've had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check whether the machine catches a loose jumper at the North Lane pole. I know that circuit well enough to spot a missed physical fault, even if I need help with the software.

say: I'd ask for **crew-tested robots** and negotiated work terms before 2034.
I'd separate **2031 thinking AI** from hands-on robots three years later.
think: At **66**, retirement remains uncertain until my pension record arrives.
Our **low savings** and Kofi's care income leave little room for a failed move.
do: Get a **pension statement** and ask the union for paid trial roles this year.
Take a **paid trial role** if offered in 2032; keep line shifts or seek inspection work in 2034.
feel: **Worried**, with time to budget but no secure retirement figure.
S3.quote: I don't feel safe enough to resign on a hopeful pension guess.
fieldNote: Hana treats **retirement at 66** as uncertain because her pension is unverified and savings remain below one month.
A **paid robot trial** could use her circuit knowledge, but she requires at least current wages and software help.

steps.text: Request a pension statement and build a low-income household budget
Ask the union to negotiate paid crew trial roles
Apply for paid inspection shifts if retirement falls short
Keep available paid line shifts when robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger lineworkers ten years is enough to build proper training and a safety rule that names who checks each machine repair. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may retire by 71, but low savings and an unknown pension make that uncertain. The gutter and utility bills are happening now, and Kofi's care shifts still move around from fortnight to fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep taking paid repairs, clear the utility arrears and request a pension statement. In 2037 Kofi and I would set a retirement date only if the low-income budget covers rent and medicine; if it doesn't, I'd apply for a posted inspection job before robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed by the robot date and still anxious about today's bills. A long runway only helps if we use it to get the account out of the red.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you save anything during the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the utility arrears are gone, I'd put ten from each actual callout into a separate reserve. I can't promise more while Kofi's shifts are uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave younger crews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark the North Lane jumper in the circuit book and tell them where the old drawing is wrong. Experience should travel with the person who takes the next shift.

say: I'd ask for **named safety checks** and training over the decade.
I'd note **2039 robots** reach field repairs when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement at **71** depends on a pension I haven't verified.
Our **current arrears** and Kofi's changing shifts keep money tight now.
do: Keep **paid repairs**, clear utility arrears and request the pension statement.
Save **ten from real callouts** after arrears clear, then review retirement or inspection work in 2037.
feel: **Less pressed** by robots, still anxious about present bills.
S4.quote: A long runway only helps if we use it to get the account out of the red.
fieldNote: Hana's **2039 robot date** offers preparation time but no relief from the current utility arrears and thin reserve.
Her **small saving step** begins only after debt clears and uses actual callout pay, not hypothetical overtime.

steps.text: Keep paid line repairs and clear utility arrears
Save ten from each actual callout after arrears are cleared
Set a 2037 retirement date only if low-income figures cover rent and medicine
Apply for a posted inspection job if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because field robots could cut my hours in 2031 while Kofi's care work is also exposed. Paid safety-inspection placements, a real pension statement, posted jobs and travel help would give us something to act on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the training replaces a wage while we take it. A certificate earned by missing rent is no bridge to the next job.

headlineQuote: A certificate earned by missing rent is no bridge to the next job.
portrait: Hana is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a vocational certificate and apprenticeship, but low pay and less than one month saved.
Her **utility arrears** make AI Plateau anxious; Kofi's changing care shifts add household income risk.
She uses **AI occasionally** for completed notes and accepts proven field tools after dispatcher and crew trials.
The **2031 robot date** alarms her because she expects major hour losses and few local inspection openings exist.
Longer warning permits **pension checks** from real callouts while she keeps paid repairs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Hana most because field robots could cut her hours while Kofi's care wages are exposed.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **paid inspection placements**, a real pension statement, posted jobs and interview travel help.
